sources.title: Bedtime Fears: Helping Overcome Them
sources.publisher: Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center (reviewed by Anne Leopard, Child Life Specialist; last updated 09/2021)
sources.quote: It is normal for young children to have fears of the dark and going to bed at night. ... Give your child a chance to tell you what makes him / her scared at bedtime. ... It may be helpful for your child to explore fears in the safety of the day. ... Begin by briefly checking and reassuring in 5 minutes, then 10 minutes, then 15 minutes, then 20 minutes until your child is asleep. ... It may be helpful for your child to have a security object
sources.supports: Fear of the dark is normal in young children; let the child tell you what scares them and explore fears in the daytime; brief check-ins at growing intervals until asleep; a security object.

sources.title: Helping Kids Overcome a Fear of the Dark
sources.publisher: Children's Hospital Colorado (expert: Benjamin Mullin, PhD, clinical child and adolescent psychologist; published 30 Jul 2025)
sources.quote: nearly 75% of children ages 4 to 12 report having nighttime fears ... I know the dark feels scary sometimes, but I also know that you can do this ... Try to stick with one dim night light, if anything. ... A calm and consistent bedtime routine can make a big difference. ... Help your child write a “contract” with their imaginary monster. ... Remind your child that a lot of fun activities can happen in the dark. ... “Making it playful is a key part of helping,” Dr. Mullin says. ... Practice being in dark spaces with your child for short periods — such as just 30 seconds — during the day. ... have that conversation earlier in the day when things are calmer. ... If your child tells you they’re scared, try to first validate their feelings
sources.supports: How common night fears are (nearly 75% of 4 to 12 year olds report them); validate first, then show confidence; one dim night light; a calm consistent routine; a playful 'contract' with the imaginary monster; making the dark playful and short daytime practice in the dark; talking about it earlier in the day.

sources.title: Nighttime Fears
sources.publisher: Seattle Children's Hospital, Sleep Medicine patient education (dated 06/01/2026)
sources.quote: It is normal for children to have nighttime fears, especially at bedtime, and most children have these at some point. ... Don't dismiss or make fun of them because fears that seem silly to an adult may be very real to a child. ... A nightlight is fine as long as it does not prevent your child from falling asleep. ... Read stories about children who are afraid and conquer their fears. ... Introduce a security object. ... If your child is anxious about your leaving their bed, check on them frequently. ... Also, it is impossible to be relaxed and scared at the same time. ... Give your child extra attention for dealing with their fears.
sources.supports: Night fears are normal and show up especially at bedtime; the fear is real to the child, so don't dismiss it; a night light is fine; read stories about children who are afraid and overcome it; a security object; check on the child often; relaxation works against fear; extra attention for coping.

sources.title: Fear of the Dark? 16 Ways to Help Your Child
sources.publisher: MGH Clay Center for Young Healthy Minds, Massachusetts General Hospital (Gene Beresin, MD, MA; undated)
sources.quote: Find a book that has a story about bedtime. ... Feelings are real and should be acknowledged even if they are afraid of monsters under their bed. ... A comfy blanket, stuffed animal or other cuddly object can help your kids soothe themselves when alone. ... Use praise and reassurance as they develop the ability to go to sleep alone.
sources.supports: Use a story about bedtime; acknowledge the feeling; a cuddly object helps the child soothe themselves; praise as the child learns to fall asleep alone.

sources.title: Nightmares
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by Amy W. Anzilotti, MD; June 2023)
sources.quote: A nightlight or a hall light can help kids feel safe in a dark room as they get ready to go back to sleep. ... A bedside flashlight can be a good nightmare-chaser. ... preschoolers and young school-age kids who have vivid imaginations ... in the daylight can help scary images lose their power

sources.title: Nighttime Fears
sources.publisher: Seattle Children's Hospital, Sleep Medicine patient education (dated 06/01/2026)
sources.quote: It is normal for children to have nighttime fears, especially at bedtime, and most children have these at some point. ... Don't dismiss or make fun of them because fears that seem silly to an adult may be very real to a child. ... A nightlight is fine as long as it does not prevent your child from falling asleep. ... Read stories about children who are afraid and conquer their fears. ... Introduce a security object. ... If your child is anxious about your leaving their bed, check on them frequently. ... Also, it is impossible to be relaxed and scared at the same time. ... Give your child extra attention for dealing with their fears.
sources.supports: Night fears are normal and show up especially at bedtime; the fear is real to the child, so don't dismiss it; a night light is fine; read stories about children who are afraid and overcome it; a security object; check on the child often; relaxation works against fear; extra attention for coping.

sources.title: Helping Kids Overcome a Fear of the Dark
sources.publisher: Children's Hospital Colorado (expert: Benjamin Mullin, PhD, clinical child and adolescent psychologist; published 30 Jul 2025)
sources.quote: nearly 75% of children ages 4 to 12 report having nighttime fears ... I know the dark feels scary sometimes, but I also know that you can do this ... Try to stick with one dim night light, if anything. ... A calm and consistent bedtime routine can make a big difference. ... Help your child write a “contract” with their imaginary monster. ... Remind your child that a lot of fun activities can happen in the dark. ... “Making it playful is a key part of helping,” Dr. Mullin says. ... Practice being in dark spaces with your child for short periods — such as just 30 seconds — during the day. ... have that conversation earlier in the day when things are calmer. ... If your child tells you they’re scared, try to first validate their feelings
sources.supports: How common night fears are (nearly 75% of 4 to 12 year olds report them); validate first, then show confidence; one dim night light; a calm consistent routine; a playful 'contract' with the imaginary monster; making the dark playful and short daytime practice in the dark; talking about it earlier in the day.

sources.title: Fear of the Dark? 16 Ways to Help Your Child
sources.publisher: MGH Clay Center for Young Healthy Minds, Massachusetts General Hospital (Gene Beresin, MD, MA; undated)
sources.quote: Find a book that has a story about bedtime. ... Feelings are real and should be acknowledged even if they are afraid of monsters under their bed. ... A comfy blanket, stuffed animal or other cuddly object can help your kids soothe themselves when alone. ... Use praise and reassurance as they develop the ability to go to sleep alone.
sources.supports: Use a story about bedtime; acknowledge the feeling; a cuddly object helps the child soothe themselves; praise as the child learns to fall asleep alone.

sources.quote: It is normal for young children to have fears of the dark and going to bed at night. ... Give your child a chance to tell you what makes him / her scared at bedtime. ... Begin by briefly checking and reassuring in 5 minutes, then 10 minutes, then 15 minutes, then 20 minutes until your child is asleep. ... It may be helpful for your child to have a security object
sources.supports: Fear of the dark is normal in young children; let the child tell you what scares them and explore fears in the daytime; brief check-ins at growing intervals until asleep; a security object.

sources.title: Helping Kids Overcome a Fear of the Dark
sources.publisher: Children's Hospital Colorado (expert: Benjamin Mullin, PhD, clinical child and adolescent psychologist; published 30 Jul 2025)
sources.quote: nearly 75% of children ages 4 to 12 report having nighttime fears ... I know the dark feels scary sometimes, but I also know that you can do this ... Try to stick with one dim night light, if anything. ... A calm and consistent bedtime routine can make a big difference. ... Help your child write a “contract” with their imaginary monster. ... Remind your child that a lot of fun activities can happen in the dark. ... “Making it playful is a key part of helping,” Dr. Mullin says. ... Practice being in dark spaces with your child for short periods — such as just 30 seconds — during the day. ... have that conversation earlier in the day when things are calmer. ... If your child tells you they’re scared, try to first validate their feelings

sources.title: Nighttime Fears
sources.publisher: Seattle Children's Hospital, Sleep Medicine patient education (dated 06/01/2026)
sources.quote: It is normal for children to have nighttime fears, especially at bedtime, and most children have these at some point. ... Don't dismiss or make fun of them because fears that seem silly to an adult may be very real to a child. ... A nightlight is fine as long as it does not prevent your child from falling asleep. ... Read stories about children who are afraid and conquer their fears. ... Introduce a security object. ... If your child is anxious about your leaving their bed, check on them frequently. ... Also, it is impossible to be relaxed and scared at the same time. ... Give your child extra attention for dealing with their fears.
sources.supports: Night fears are normal and show up especially at bedtime; the fear is real to the child, so don't dismiss it; a night light is fine; read stories about children who are afraid and overcome it; a security object; check on the child often; relaxation works against fear; extra attention for coping.

sources.title: Helping Kids Overcome a Fear of the Dark
sources.publisher: Children's Hospital Colorado (expert: Benjamin Mullin, PhD, clinical child and adolescent psychologist; published 30 Jul 2025)
sources.quote: nearly 75% of children ages 4 to 12 report having nighttime fears ... I know the dark feels scary sometimes, but I also know that you can do this ... Try to stick with one dim night light, if anything. ... A calm and consistent bedtime routine can make a big difference. ... Help your child write a “contract” with their imaginary monster. ... Remind your child that a lot of fun activities can happen in the dark. ... “Making it playful is a key part of helping,” Dr. Mullin says. ... Practice being in dark spaces with your child for short periods — such as just 30 seconds — during the day. ... have that conversation earlier in the day when things are calmer. ... If your child tells you they’re scared, try to first validate their feelings
sources.supports: How common night fears are (nearly 75% of 4 to 12 year olds report them); validate first, then show confidence; one dim night light; a calm consistent routine; a playful 'contract' with the imaginary monster; making the dark playful and short daytime practice in the dark; talking about it earlier in the day.

sources.title: Fear of the Dark? 16 Ways to Help Your Child
sources.publisher: MGH Clay Center for Young Healthy Minds, Massachusetts General Hospital (Gene Beresin, MD, MA; undated)
sources.quote: Find a book that has a story about bedtime. ... Feelings are real and should be acknowledged even if they are afraid of monsters under their bed. ... A comfy blanket, stuffed animal or other cuddly object can help your kids soothe themselves when alone. ... Use praise and reassurance as they develop the ability to go to sleep alone.
sources.supports: Use a story about bedtime; acknowledge the feeling; a cuddly object helps the child soothe themselves; praise as the child learns to fall asleep alone.
